scenes.heading: Ageing and cell death
scenes.sub: Why your cells are built to die on cue
scenes.say: Your fingers separated before you were born because the cells between them died on cue. Millions of your cells die every day. So how do cells die, why do they age, and how does cancer escape both limits?

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Hard rubbish night: the couch is put out neatly and taken away
scenes.science: Apoptosis: the cell packs itself up and phagocytes remove it
scenes.breaks: Apoptosis is something the cell actively does using ATP, and the 'eat me' signal is moved to the outer membrane face, not added.
scenes.say: Think of hard rubbish night. You put the old couch out neatly and the truck takes it away with no mess. That's apoptosis: the cell packs itself into apoptotic bodies and shows an eat me signal, so phagocytes remove it with no inflammation. Necrosis is like a wheelie bin that splits open in the street. Everything spills, and that causes inflammation.

scenes.heading: Apoptosis vs necrosis
scenes.say: A handy check: shrink and pack, or swell and burst? Apoptosis is programmed and needs ATP. The cell shrinks and its contents are packaged up, so there's no inflammation. Necrosis follows severe injury, like loss of blood supply. The cell swells, the membrane bursts, and the spill triggers inflammation.

scenes.heading: The caspase pathways
scenes.say: Apoptosis is carried out by caspases, protein-cutting enzymes. Remember: eight from outside, nine from inside, both meet at three. A death receptor switches on caspase eight. Stress inside the cell releases cytochrome c from mitochondria, which activates caspase nine. Both switch on executioner caspase three. The cascade amplifies the signal and makes the decision irreversible.

scenes.heading: Telomeres and senescence
points: Telomeres: TTAGGG repeats at chromosome ends
End-replication problem: they shorten each copy
scenes.say: Telomeres are repeated DNA at the ends of chromosomes, like the plastic tips on shoelaces. Because of the end-replication problem, they shorten a little every time DNA is copied. When they get critically short, the cell enters senescence. It's still alive, but it permanently stops dividing. The enzyme telomerase can add the repeats back.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Telomeres are 9 kb at doubling 10 and 6 kb at doubling 40. Cells senesce at about 4 kb. How many more doublings?
scenes.say: Telomeres drop from nine to six kilobases over thirty doublings. That's three thousand base pairs over thirty, or one hundred base pairs per doubling. Senescence happens at about four kilobases, so two thousand base pairs are left. Two thousand divided by one hundred gives about twenty more doublings.
scenes.caption: Telomeres drop from 9 to 6 kb over 30 doublings: 3000 bp ÷ 30 = 100 bp per doubling. Senescence happens at about 4 kb, so 2000 bp are left. 2000 ÷ 100 gives about 20 more doublings.

scenes.heading: Cancer: accelerator and brakes
scenes.say: Cancer is loss of control over division and death. An oncogene is a stuck accelerator: one mutated copy is enough. A tumour suppressor like T P fifty-three is the brakes, and usually both copies must be lost. Cancer cells also evade apoptosis and switch telomerase back on to become immortal.
scenes.caption: Cancer is loss of control over division and death. An oncogene is a stuck accelerator: one mutated copy is enough. A tumour suppressor like TP53 is the brakes, and usually both copies must be lost. Cancer cells also evade apoptosis and switch telomerase back on to become immortal.

points: Apoptosis: shrink and pack, no inflammation
Cancer: oncogenes on, tumour suppressors off
scenes.say: Quick recap. Apoptosis is tidy, necrosis is messy. Caspase eight from outside, nine from inside, both meet at three. Short telomeres trigger senescence. And cancer comes from oncogenes switched on and tumour suppressors lost. Now try the practice questions!
